## Introduction

This project investigates differences in gene expression between dexamethasone-treated and untreated human airway smooth muscle cells using a publicly available RNA-seq dataset.
```{r}
# load the installed airway package 
library(airway)
# loads the RNA-seq dataset in R
data(airway)
dim(airway) # shows the dimensions of the dataset how many rows and columns 
airway
```
## assay(airway) — Gene expression counts.
colData(airway) — Information about each sample, such as treatment status.
rowData(airway) — Information about the genes.
assays — The experimental measurements stored in the dataset. (1) — There is one assay (one measurement matrix) stored.
counts — The name of that assay. It contains the number of sequencing reads assigned to each gene in each sample

```{r}
# retrieve the count matrix and selects row 1-5 and all columns 
assay(airway)[1:5, ]
```


```{r}
# col for columns and data for info about the samples  
#metadata - meaning data about data
colData(airway)
# trt treated with dexamethasone untrt is control 
```
## Research question: 
"How does dexamethasone treatment affect gene expression?"
```{r}
# know which smaples belong to each group before comparing their gene expression
table(colData(airway)$dex) # selects the colum named dex
```
```{r}
# check gene info
rowData(airway)
```
## DESeq2

```{r}
library(DESeq2)
# name the new line deseqdataset, the input is from airway and the design we want is dex 
dds <- DESeqDataSet(airway, design = ~ dex)

dds <- DESeq(dds)
# DESeq2 considers both the magnitude of gene expression changes and variability between samples.
res <- results(dds)

head(res)
summary(res)
resultsNames(dds)
```
# 
basemean - average normalized expression, log2FoldChange - how much expression changed in which direction. lfcSE - uncertainty in the extimated log2 fold change. stat- statistical test statistic, p-value - evidence aginst no difference, padj - p-value adjusted fro multiple testing
LFC log fold change 

```{r}
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("dex", "trt", "untrt"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)
```

```{r}
#store the data as R data frame
res_df <- as.data.frame(res)

#filter significant genes 
sig_genes <- res_df[res_df$padj < 0.05 & !is.na(res_df$padj), ]

nrow(sig_genes)
```

```{r}
#create a separate data frame that excludes genes with missing adjusted p-values.

plot_df <- na.omit(res_df)

nrow(plot_df)
```
## Volcano plot 
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj))) + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05)) +  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1))
```


```{r}
plot_df$Significance <- "Not Significant"
```


```{r}
# identify upregulated genes 
plot_df$Significance[ plot_df$padj < 0.05 & plot_df$log2FoldChange > 1] <- "Upregulated"
table(plot_df$Significance)

plot_df$Significance[plot_df$padj < 0.05 & plot_df$log2FoldChange < -1] <- "Downregulated"
table(plot_df$Significance)

```

```{r}
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = Significance)) + geom_point() + scale_color_manual(values = c("Upregulated" = "red", "Downregulated" = "blue","Not Significant" = "grey"  )) + labs(
    title = "Effect of Dexamethasone on Gene Expression",
    x = "Log2 Fold Change (Treated vs Untreated)",
    y = "-Log10 Adjusted P-value",
    color = "Gene Category"
  ) + theme_minimal()

ggsave("figures/volcano_plot.png", width = 8, height = 6)
```

## PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
Do the treated and untreated samples show different overall gene expression patterns?
Volcano plot → Each dot represents a gene.
PCA plot → Each dot represents a sample.
Prepare data using Variance Stabilizing Transformation (VST).
vst() transforms the normalized gene-count data so that genes with very high counts don't dominate the analysis simply because of their greater variability.
VST reduces this dependence between the mean and variance, making the data more suitable for PCA.

```{r}
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)
```


```{r}
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "dex")
```
PC1 (Principal Component 1): Captures the largest source of variation between samples.
PC1 = 44% means that PC1 explains 44% of the variation represented in the data used for PCA.
PC2 (Principal Component 2): Captures the second-largest source of variation, independently of PC1.
PC2 = 25% means that PC2 explains another 25%.
total = 69% the two axes summarize 69% of variation in the data 

```{r}
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = "cell")
```


```{r}
design(dds) <- ~ cell + dex
```


```{r}
dds <- DESeq(dds)
```


```{r}
res <- results(dds,
               contrast = c("dex", "trt", "untrt"),
               alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)
```


```{r}
res_df <- as.data.frame(res)

head(res_df)
plot_df <- na.omit(res_df)

```

```{r}
plot_df$Significance <- "Not Significant"

# identify upregulated genes 
plot_df$Significance[ plot_df$padj < 0.05 & plot_df$log2FoldChange > 1] <- "Upregulated"

plot_df$Significance[plot_df$padj < 0.05 & plot_df$log2FoldChange < -1] <- "Downregulated"
table(plot_df$Significance)
```

## Volcano Plot

```{r}

unique(plot_df$Significance)
```


```{r}
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = Significance)) + geom_point() + scale_color_manual(values = c("Upregulated" = "red", "Downregulated" = "blue","Not Significant" = "grey"  )) + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05),
           linetype = "dashed") +
geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1),
```

The volcano plot helps to identify individual genes showing statistically significant expression changes.

Are certain biological processes overrepresented among the genes that changed?
```{r}
# create a list of genese satisfying the significance criteria
sig_genes <- rownames(res_df)[  !is.na(res_df$padj) & res_df$padj < 0.05]
length(sig_genes)
head(sig_genes)
```

DESeq2 identifies which genes changed significantly. GO enrichment identifies which biological processes are overrepresented among those genes. 

```{r}
library(AnnotationDbi) #Helps translate gene identifiers
library(org.Hs.eg.db) #Provides human gene annotations
library(clusterProfiler) #Performs GO enrichment analysis
```

###

Ensembl ID: Used by the Ensembl database.
Entrez Gene ID: Used by NCBI Gene.
Gene symbol: A recognizable name, such as TP53
```{r}
entrez_genes <- mapIds(
  org.Hs.eg.db,
  keys = sig_genes,
  column = "ENTREZID",
  keytype = "ENSEMBL",
  multiVals = "first" #If multiple matches exist, return the first
)
head(entrez_genes)
entrez_genes <- na.omit(entrez_genes) # for Ensembl IDs that might not have a corresponding Entrez ID

length(entrez_genes)
```

```{r}
length(unique(entrez_genes))
```
##Prepare background genes for GO enrichment
Compare 
Significant genes: Genes that changed significantly after dexamethasone treatment.
with 
Background genes: All eligible genes, including significant and non-significant genes.

```{r}
background_genes <- rownames(res_df)[!is.na(res_df$pvalue)]
length(background_genes)
```
** How common is a biological process among our significant genes compared with how common it is among all eligible genes? **
```{r}
background_entrez <- mapIds(
  org.Hs.eg.db, keys = background_genes, column = "ENTREZID", keytype = "ENSEMBL", multiVals = "first")
background_entrez <- na.omit(background_entrez)
length(background_entrez)
```

```{r}
background_entrez <- unique(background_entrez)
length(background_entrez)
```
# checks whether each significant Entrez ID appears in the background list.
```{r}
# checks whether each significant Entrez ID appears in the background list.
sum(entrez_genes %in% background_entrez)
```

## Run GO enrichment
the GO has 3 categories 
### Biological Process BP 
### Molecular Function MF
### Cellular Component CC
BH Controls the False Discovery Rate (most common in RNA-seq)
```{r}
# use the enrichGO() function from clusterProfiler

ego <- enrichGO(
  gene = entrez_genes,  # sig genes
  universe = background_entrez,  # background genes 
  OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db, # Human gene annotation database
  keyType = "ENTREZID",
  ont = "BP", # Analyze Biological Processes
  pAdjustMethod = "BH", # Adjust p-values using Benjamini–Hochberg
  pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
  qvalueCutoff = 0.05,
  readable = TRUE #Display gene symbols instead of Entrez IDs in the enrichment results
)
ego
```
These results suggest that genes associated with blood-vessel formation and extracellular matrix organization are particularly overrepresented among the differentially expressed genes.

```{r}
dotplot(ego, showCategory = 10, label_format = 35)
```

Genes associated with angiogenesis, extracellular matrix organization, and cytoskeletal organization are significantly enriched among the differentially expressed genes. 

GO enrichment results show that genes associated with angiogenesis and actin filament organization are overrepresented among our differentially expressed genes.

It does not tell us whether those biological processes increased or decreased in activity.
GO Biological Process enrichment analysis identified 572 significantly enriched terms among the differentially expressed genes. Prominent terms included angiogenesis, extracellular matrix organization, and actin filament organization. These findings suggest that dexamethasone treatment is associated with transcriptional changes involving cellular organization, adhesion, and signaling. However, enrichment analysis alone does not establish whether these processes are activated or suppressed.

```{r}
ggsave("figures/GO_dotplot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

## Biological interpretation
Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels from existing blood vessels.
It is important for:Tissue growth and repair, Wound healing, Supplying tissues with oxygen and nutrients. Certain diseases, including cancer.
The	Result shows: 
Biological process	Angiogenesis
GeneRatio	186/3406
FoldEnrichment	1.71
Adjusted p-value	4.03 × 10⁻¹²

This means genes associated with angiogenesis are significantly overrepresented among the differentially expressed genes.

## Results

### Differential Gene Expression Analysis

Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 to compare dexamethasone-treated and untreated human airway smooth muscle cells while accounting for differences between cell lines.

Using an adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05, 4,028 genes were identified as significantly differentially expressed. Of these, 2,211 were upregulated and 1,817 were downregulated following dexamethasone treatment.

### Principal Component Analysis

Principal component analysis (PCA) showed separation between treated and untreated samples along PC1, which explained 44% of the variation. PC2 explained an additional 25% of the variation. Differences between cell lines also appeared to contribute to sample variation.

### Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis

GO Biological Process enrichment analysis identified 572 significantly enriched terms. Prominent processes included angiogenesis, extracellular matrix organization, and actin filament organization.

These findings suggest that dexamethasone treatment is associated with changes in genes involved in cellular structure, extracellular matrix organization, and signaling. However, enrichment alone does not establish whether these biological processes were activated or inhibited.


### Discussion 
### Extracellular Matrix Organization

GO enrichment analysis identified extracellular matrix organization as one of the significantly enriched biological processes following dexamethasone treatment. This suggests that dexamethasone is associated with transcriptional changes in genes involved in extracellular matrix organization, cell adhesion, and structural support.

Because the enrichment analysis included both upregulated and downregulated genes, these findings do not establish whether extracellular matrix organization was activated or suppressed. Further experimental validation, such as immunofluorescence imaging or measurement of extracellular matrix proteins, would be needed to determine whether these transcriptional changes result in alterations to extracellular matrix structure or function.
